claim: X. laevis is an allotetraploid that arose from hybridization of two diploid species ~18 million years ago.
source: Xenopus laevis, an allotetraploid that arose from hybridization of two diploid species ~18 million years ago
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Session et al., 2016 in the introduction.

claim: The two ancestral diploid species that hybridized to form X. laevis were separated by ~34 million years.
source: X. laevis's L (long) and S (short) subgenomes are inherited from each of two distinct species separated by ~34 million years that hybridized ~18 million years ago (Session et al., 2016; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated in the introduction with citation to Session et al., 2016.

claim: Most genes in X. laevis are retained as two homeologous copies.
source: Although most genes have been retained as two homeologous copies, we find that a majority of them undergo asymmetric activation in the early embryo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2A showing 57% of genes are present on both subgenomes.

claim: A majority of homeologous gene pairs undergo asymmetric activation in the early X. laevis embryo.
source: Although most genes have been retained as two homeologous copies, we find that a majority of them undergo asymmetric activation in the early embryo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by RNA-seq data in Figure 2B-C showing differential homeolog expression.

claim: There are extensive differences in predicted enhancer architecture between the X. laevis L and S subgenomes.
source: Chromatin accessibility profiling and CUT&RUN for modified histones and transcription factor binding reveal extensive differences in predicted enhancer architecture between the subgenomes
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN data in Figure 3.

claim: Differences in enhancer architecture between X. laevis subgenomes likely arose through genomic disruptions as a consequence of allotetraploidy.
source: Chromatin accessibility profiling and CUT&RUN for modified histones and transcription factor binding reveal extensive differences in predicted enhancer architecture between the subgenomes, which likely arose through genomic disruptions as a consequence of allotetraploidy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the data, representing an inference from the observed enhancer differences.

claim: Combined divergent homeolog contributions in X. laevis result in embryonic gene expression levels that are broadly conserved with diploid X. tropicalis.
source: However, comparison with diploid X. tropicalis and zebrafish shows broad conservation of embryonic gene expression levels when divergent homeolog contributions are combined
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by comparative RNA-seq analysis in Figure 5A showing Spearman's ρ=0.67 for combined L+S expression vs X. tropicalis.

claim: There is strong selection to maintain dosage in the core vertebrate pluripotency transcriptional program in X. laevis.
source: comparison with diploid X. tropicalis and zebrafish shows broad conservation of embryonic gene expression levels when divergent homeolog contributions are combined, implying strong selection to maintain dosage in the core vertebrate pluripotency transcriptional program, amid genomic instability following hybridization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the comparative expression data, representing an inference about evolutionary selection.

claim: Zygotic genome activation in X. laevis is triggered after an initial period of transcriptional quiescence following fertilization.
source: In animals, zygotic genome activation (ZGA) is triggered after an initial period of transcriptional quiescence following fertilization of the egg, during the maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT; Lee et al., 2014; Vastenhouw et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Lee et al., 2014 and Vastenhouw et al., 2019.

claim: In mammals, zygotic genome activation occurs during the slow first cleavages.
source: In mammals, this occurs during the slow first cleavages (Svoboda, 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Svoboda, 2018.

claim: Mammalian pluripotent stem cells in the blastocyst are induced by a core network of factors including NANOG, OCT4, and SOX2.
source: a few days removed from the subsequent induction of pluripotent stem cells in the blastocyst by a core network of factors including NANOG, OCT4, and SOX2 (Li and Belmonte, 2017; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Li and Belmonte, 2017 and Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2016.

claim: Zebrafish, Xenopus, and Drosophila activate their genomes in the blastula hours after fertilization.
source: In contrast, faster-dividing taxa including zebrafish, Xenopus, and Drosophila activate their genomes in the blastula hours after fertilization (Foe and Alberts, 1983; Kane and Kimmel, 1993; Newport and Kirschner, 1982a; Vastenhouw et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: In zebrafish, maternally provided homologs of NANOG, OCT4, and SOX2 are required for a large share of genome activation.
source: In zebrafish, maternally provided homologs of NANOG, OCT4, and SOX2 are required for a large share of genome activation (Lee et al., 2013; Leichsenring et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2022)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Lee et al., 2013; Leichsenring et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2022.

claim: Vertebrate embryos deploy conserved pluripotency induction mechanisms at different times during early development.
source: thus, vertebrate embryos deploy conserved pluripotency induction mechanisms at different times during early development.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion drawn from the comparison of mammalian and zebrafish/Xenopus development.

claim: Zelda, CLAMP, and GAF are maternal factors that direct genome activation and stem cell induction in Drosophila.
source: Beyond vertebrates, unrelated maternal factors direct genome activation and the induction of stem cells, for example Zelda (Liang et al., 2008), CLAMP (Colonnetta et al., 2021; Duan et al., 2021), and GAF (Gaskill et al., 2021) in Drosophila
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Drosophila maternal factors Zelda, CLAMP, and GAF share functional aspects with vertebrate pluripotency factors, including pioneering roles in opening repressed embryonic chromatin.
source: although they seem to share many functional aspects with vertebrate pluripotency factors, including pioneering roles in opening repressed embryonic chromatin and establishing activating histone modifications (Blythe and Wieschaus, 2016; Gaskill et al., 2021; Hug et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Blythe and Wieschaus, 2016; Gaskill et al., 2021; Hug et al., 2017.

claim: The gene network regulating pluripotency has been extensively modified over evolutionary time.
source: This diversity of strategies implies that the gene network regulating pluripotency has been extensively modified over evolutionary time (Endo et al., 2020; Fernandez-Tresguerres et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the diversity of ZGA mechanisms, with citations to Endo et al., 2020 and Fernandez-Tresguerres et al., 2010.

claim: A subsequent whole-genome duplication after hybridization restored meiotic pairing in X. laevis.
source: A subsequent whole-genome duplication restored meiotic pairing.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as part of the description of X. laevis evolutionary history.

claim: Despite extensive rearrangements and deletions, most X. laevis genes are still encoded as two copies (homeologs) on parallel, non-inter-recombining chromosomes.
source: Despite extensive rearrangements and deletions, most genes are still encoded as two copies (homeologs) on parallel, non-inter-recombining chromosomes (Session et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Session et al., 2016.

claim: The recent high-quality X. laevis genome assembly has made it feasible to resolve differential expression and regulation genome-wide between the two subgenomes.
source: however, the recent high-quality X. laevis genome assembly has made it feasible to resolve differential expression and regulation genome-wide between the two subgenomes (Elurbe et al., 2017; Session et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Elurbe et al., 2017 and Session et al., 2016.

claim: Allopolyploidy often provokes acute effects on gene expression.
source: Allopolyploidy often provokes acute effects on gene expression (Hu and Wendel, 2019; Moran et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Hu and Wendel, 2019 and Moran et al., 2021.

claim: Allopolyploidy leads to regulatory shifts over time to reconcile dosage imbalances and incompatibilities between gene copies.
source: leading to regulatory shifts over time to reconcile dosage imbalances and incompatibilities between gene copies (Grover et al., 2012; Song et al., 2020; Swamy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Grover et al., 2012; Song et al., 2020; Swamy et al., 2021.

claim: There is a broad trend toward balanced homeolog expression across X. laevis development and adult tissues.
source: For X. laevis, there is a broad trend toward balanced homeolog expression across development and adult tissues, with a subtle bias in favor of the L homeolog that emerges after genome activation (Session et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Session et al., 2016.

claim: There is a subtle bias in favor of the L homeolog that emerges after genome activation in X. laevis.
source: with a subtle bias in favor of the L homeolog that emerges after genome activation (Session et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Session et al., 2016.

claim: X. laevis has an overall ontogenetic and transcriptomic trajectory similar to diploid X. tropicalis.
source: and an overall ontogenetic and transcriptomic trajectory similar to 48 million-years diverged diploid X. tropicalis (Harland and Grainger, 2011; Yanai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Harland and Grainger, 2011 and Yanai et al., 2011.

claim: X. laevis and X. tropicalis diverged 48 million years ago.
source: similar to 48 million-years diverged diploid X. tropicalis (Harland and Grainger, 2011; Yanai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: X. laevis exhibits differential homeologous enhancer activity in the eye.
source: Initial observations in X. laevis have demonstrated differential homeologous enhancer activity in the eye (Ochi et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Ochi et al., 2017.

claim: X. laevis has a divergent cis-regulatory landscape of histone modifications and recruitment of transcriptional machinery in the early gastrula.
source: and a divergent cis-regulatory landscape of histone modifications and recruitment of transcriptional machinery in the early gastrula (Elurbe et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Elurbe et al., 2017.

claim: Embryonic genome activation is likely asymmetric between the two X. laevis subgenomes.
source: suggesting that embryonic genome activation is likely also asymmetric between the two subgenomes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from previous observations of differential enhancer activity and cis-regulatory landscapes.

claim: ZGA regulators have not previously been identified in X. laevis.
source: Although Xenopus embryos have long been a model for understanding the MZT, for example (Amodeo et al., 2015; Charney et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019b; Gentsch et al., 2019; Gibeaux et al., 2018; Gurdon et al., 1958; Kimelman et al., 1987; Newport and Kirschner, 1982a; Newport and Kirschner, 1982b; Paraiso et al., 2019; Skirkanich et al., 2011; Veenstra et al., 1999; Yanai et al., 2011), ZGA regulators have not previously been identified in X. laevis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in knowledge.

claim: Maternal Pou5f3 and Sox3 are top-level regulators of X. laevis pluripotency and ZGA.
source: Here, we identify maternal Pou5f3 and Sox3 as top-level regulators of X. laevis pluripotency and ZGA
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a main finding, supported by morpholino knockdown and CUT&RUN data in Figure 4.

claim: Predicted enhancer architecture differentially recruits Pou5f3 and Sox3 to homeologous gene copies between the two X. laevis subgenomes.
source: and elucidate the predicted enhancer architecture that differentially recruits them to homeologous gene copies between the two subgenomes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a main finding, supported by CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Despite differential subgenome activation, combined transcriptional output in X. laevis converges to proportionally resemble the diploid state.
source: Despite differential subgenome activation, combined transcriptional output converges to proportionally resemble the diploid state, maintaining gene dosage for the embryonic pluripotency program.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a main finding, supported by comparative transcriptome analysis in Figure 5.

claim: 4772 genes show significant activation by the middle of stage 9 in X. laevis.
source: culminating in 4772 genes with significant activation by the middle of stage 9 (8 hours post fertilization [h.p.f.] at 23 °C) (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Two-thirds of activated genes in X. laevis have substantial maternal contributions that mask their activation when quantifying exon-overlapping reads alone.
source: indeed, two-thirds of these genes had substantial maternal contributions that masked their activation when quantifying exon-overlapping reads alone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data comparing exon and intron signal in Figure 1C.

claim: Activated genes in X. laevis fail to be activated in embryos treated with triptolide.
source: These genes fail to be activated in embryos treated at 1 cell (stage 1) with the transcription inhibitor triptolide (Gibeaux et al., 2018) when compared to DMSO vehicle control embryos (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 2662 genes (56% of all activated genes) represent the first wave of genome activation in X. laevis.
source: A total of 2662 genes (56% of all activated genes) were still significantly activated in cycloheximide-treated embryos compared to triptolide-treated embryos, representing the first wave of genome activation in the embryo (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data comparing cycloheximide and triptolide treatments in Figure 1C.

claim: Activated genes in X. laevis are preferentially encoded as two homeologous copies in the genome.
source: We analyzed subgenome of origin for activated genes and found that they are preferentially encoded as two homeologous copies in the genome (p=2.3 × 10–225, χ-squared test, 10 d.o.f.; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A majority of X. laevis homeolog pairs experience asymmetric expression during genome activation.
source: However, a majority of these genes have asymmetric expression between the two homeologs, often with transcription deriving from only the L or S copy alone (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Asymmetry in homeolog expression is more pronounced at stage 8 but balances somewhat as genome activation progresses.
source: This asymmetry is more pronounced at stage 8, but balances somewhat as genome activation progresses, suggesting timing differences for homeolog activation that could result from subtle regulatory divergence (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Homeolog expression asymmetry is slightly less pronounced for strictly zygotic genes compared to maternal-zygotic genes.
source: and slightly less pronounced for strictly zygotic genes compared to maternal-zygotic genes (maternal contribution ≥1 TPM; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Maternal-zygotic genes are often reactivated with different homeolog expression patterns compared to their maternal contribution.
source: which are often reactivated with different homeolog expression patterns compared to their maternal contribution (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 2E.

claim: A heightened imbalance in favor of the L homeolog emerges after genome activation in differentiated cell lineages.
source: After genome activation, a heightened imbalance in favor of the L homeolog emerges, as measured by activation patterns in four differentiated cell lineages (Johnson et al., 2022; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–I)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data from Johnson et al., 2022 shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–I.

claim: For one-third of genes activated in more than one lineage, different homeologs are activated in different lineages.
source: Indeed, for one-third of genes activated in more than one lineage, different homeologs are activated in different lineages (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Genes activated from both subgenomes are enriched in transcriptional regulators.
source: Genes activated from both subgenomes are enriched in transcriptional regulators (p<0.01, Fisher's exact test, two-sided) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: There is no evidence for stronger functional divergence between homeologs expressed asymmetrically between the subgenomes, as estimated by dN/dS ratio.
source: However, there is no evidence for stronger functional divergence between homeologs expressed asymmetrically between the subgenomes, as estimated by non-synonymous versus synonymous mutation rate in coding regions (dN/dS ratio; Figure 2—figure supplement 1K and L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by dN/dS analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: mir-427 is one of the most strongly activated genes in the X. laevis embryonic genome.
source: Similar to X. tropicalis mir-427 (Owens et al., 2016) and the related zebrafish mir-430 (Lee et al., 2013), mir-427 is one of the most strongly activated genes in the X. laevis embryonic genome (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplements 1C and 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplements 1C and 2A.

claim: The mir-427 precursor hairpin sequence is found in five copies overlapping a Xenbase-annotated long non-coding RNA on chr1L in version 9.2 of the X. laevis genome assembly.
source: In version 9.2 of the X. laevis genome assembly, the miR-427 precursor hairpin sequence is found in only five copies overlapping a Xenbase-annotated long non-coding RNA on chr1L (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by genome alignment data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The mir-427 locus on Chr1L in the v10.1 X. laevis genome assembly is composed of 33 precursor copies encoded in both strand orientations over 55 kilobases.
source: This revealed an expanded mir-427 locus at the distal end of Chr1L composed of 33 precursor copies, encoded in both strand orientations over 55 kilobases (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by genome alignment data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The corresponding region on Chr1S to the mir-427 locus is unalignable.
source: The corresponding region on Chr1S is unalignable (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that mir-427 is encoded on only the L subgenome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by genome alignment data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: mir-427 is encoded on only the L subgenome in X. laevis.
source: The corresponding region on Chr1S is unalignable (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that mir-427 is encoded on only the L subgenome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the unalignable Chr1S region, supported by genome alignment data.

claim: Two mir-427 hairpin sequence matches are found on the distal end of Chr3S, but these loci are not supported by substantial RNA-seq coverage.
source: We additionally found two mir-427 hairpin sequence matches to the distal end of Chr3S, but these loci were not supported by substantial RNA-seq coverage (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by genome alignment and RNA-seq data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: X. tropicalis encodes 171 tandemly arrayed mir-427 precursors on the distal end of Chr03.
source: This is reminiscent of the X. tropicalis mir-427 genomic configuration (Owens et al., 2016), although smaller in scale and on a non-homologous chromosome. In X. tropicalis, 171 tandemly arrayed mir-427 precursors are found on the distal end of Chr03
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Owens et al., 2016.

claim: The large array of mir-427 precursors in X. tropicalis is thought to accelerate mature miR-427 accumulation during the MZT to facilitate rapid maternal clearance.
source: which is thought to accelerate mature miR-427 accumulation during the MZT to facilitate rapid maternal clearance (Owens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Owens et al., 2016.

claim: Zebrafish encodes a large array of more than 2000 mir-430 precursors.
source: Zebrafish similarly encodes a large array of more than 2000 mir-430 precursors, which begin to target maternal mRNA for clearance shortly after ZGA (Bazzini et al., 2012; Giraldez et al., 2006; Hadzhiev et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The mir-427 locus has undergone genomic remodeling, resulting in absence from the S subgenome.
source: These results strongly suggest that the mir-427 locus has undergone genomic remodeling, resulting in absence from the S subgenome, but possibly also translocation between chromosomes in the tropicalis or laevis lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the genomic configuration differences.

claim: The mir-427 locus may have undergone translocation between chromosomes in the tropicalis or laevis lineages.
source: These results strongly suggest that the mir-427 locus has undergone genomic remodeling, resulting in absence from the S subgenome, but possibly also translocation between chromosomes in the tropicalis or laevis lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as speculation based on the different chromosomal locations in X. laevis and X. tropicalis.

claim: Cell dissociation is necessary for efficient nuclear isolation to carry out CUT&RUN chemistry in X. laevis blastulae.
source: We found that cell dissociation was necessary for efficient nuclear isolation to carry out the on-bead CUT&RUN chemistry (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K27ac are enriched in the TSS regions of activated genes at stages 8 and 9.
source: At stages 8 and 9, the active marks H3 lysine 4 trimethylation (H3K4me3) and H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac) were enriched in the transcription start site (TSS) regions of activated genes
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by CUT&RUN data in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Differential homeolog activation measured by RNA-seq significantly correlates with differential histone modification profiles.
source: and differential homeolog activation measured by RNA-seq significantly correlates with differential histone modification profiles, with a slight overall bias toward stronger L homeolog chromatin activity (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by CUT&RUN and RNA-seq data in Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: There is a slight overall bias toward stronger L homeolog chromatin activity.
source: with a slight overall bias toward stronger L homeolog chromatin activity (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by CUT&RUN data in Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: No promoter sequence differences between homeologs would implicate differential recruitment of specific transcription factors.
source: However, we found no promoter sequence differences between homeologs that would implicate differential recruitment of specific transcription factors (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by motif analysis in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Accessible chromatin is already evident at stage 8 in putative enhancer regions.
source: Accessible chromatin is already evident at stage 8 in putative enhancer regions, though the overall signal is weak, and by stage 9, these regions exhibit robust accessibility (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ATAC-seq data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 15,654 putative open and acetylated gene-distal regulatory regions are present at genome activation in X. laevis.
source: This yielded 15,654 putative open and acetylated gene-distal regulatory regions at genome activation
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN data analysis.

claim: 5047 high confidence predicted enhancers were identified in X. laevis at genome activation.
source: of which we classified 5047 as high confidence predicted enhancers that had ≥2 fold signal enrichment in each of at least three H3K27ac replicates and three ATAC-seq replicates individually (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 79% of predicted enhancer regions successfully lifted over to homeologous chromosomes.
source: Seventy-nine percent of predicted enhancer regions successfully lifted over to homeologous chromosomes
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by genome alignment analysis.

claim: >92% of lifted-over enhancers are flanked by the same homeologous genes.
source: and of these, >92% of these are flanked by the same homeologous genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), confirming local synteny.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by synteny analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Only 21% of paired regions involving high-confidence predicted enhancers had conserved activity in both homeologs.
source: Among the paired regions involving high-confidence predicted enhancers, only 21% had conserved activity in both homeologs, with the remaining pairs exhibiting differential H3K27ac and chromatin accessibility (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq data in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Differential predicted enhancer density around genes significantly correlated with differential activation.
source: Differential predicted enhancer density around genes significantly correlated with differential activation (p=1.3 × 10–16, Pearson's correlation test; Figure 3C, middle, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis of enhancer density and RNA-seq data in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Conserved enhancers had equivalent density near both homeologs regardless of activation status.
source: In contrast, conserved enhancers had equivalent density near both homeologs regardless of activation status (p=0.67, Pearson's correlation test; Figure 3C, right).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: Differences in enhancer activity likely underlie divergent gene homeolog transcription at genome activation.
source: Thus, differences in enhancer activity likely underlie divergent gene homeolog transcription at genome activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the correlation between differential enhancer activity and differential gene activation.

claim: OCT4 and SOX2/3 binding motifs are strongly enriched in both active L enhancers and active S enhancers.
source: Two motifs were strongly enriched in both active L enhancers and active S enhancers, corresponding to the binding sequences of the pluripotency factors OCT4 and SOX2/3 (SOXB1 family; Figure 3F, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by motif enrichment analysis in Figure 3F and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Mammalian OCT4 and SOX2 are master regulators of pluripotent stem cell induction.
source: Since mammalian OCT4 and SOX2 are master regulators of pluripotent stem cell induction (Li and Belmonte, 2017; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Li and Belmonte, 2017 and Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2016.

claim: Zebrafish homologs of OCT4 and SOX2 are maternally provided and required for embryonic genome activation.
source: and zebrafish homologs of these factors are maternally provided and required for embryonic genome activation (Lee et al., 2013; Leichsenring et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2022)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Lee et al., 2013; Leichsenring et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2022.

claim: Differential enhancer binding by maternal X. laevis OCT4 and SOXB1 homologs underlies asymmetric activation of the L and S subgenomes.
source: we hypothesized that differential enhancer binding by maternal X. laevis OCT4 and SOXB1 homologs underlies asymmetric activation of the L and S subgenomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis based on motif enrichment and prior knowledge.

claim: RNA-seq confirms high maternal levels of sox3 and pou5f3.3 mRNA in X. laevis.
source: RNA-seq confirms high maternal levels of sox3 and pou5f3.3 (OCT4 homolog) mRNA, as well as lower levels of paralog pou5f3.2, each deriving from both subgenomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Combinations of pou5f3.3+sox3 morpholinos led to mild gastrulation defects in X. laevis.
source: Combinations of pou5f3.3+sox3 morpholinos and pou5f3.2+pou5 f3.3 morpholinos led to mild and severe gastrulation defects, respectively
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phenotypic observations in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Combinations of pou5f3.2+pou5f3.3 morpholinos led to severe gastrulation defects in X. laevis.
source: Combinations of pou5f3.3+sox3 morpholinos and pou5f3.2+pou5 f3.3 morpholinos led to mild and severe gastrulation defects, respectively
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phenotypic observations in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Combining all three morpholinos (pou5f3.2, pou5f3.3, and sox3) led to developmental arrest with a complete failure to close the blastopore.
source: while combining all three morpholinos led to developmental arrest with a complete failure to close the blastopore (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phenotypic observations in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pou5f3/Sox3 morpholino phenotypes in X. laevis are consistent with what has been reported in X. tropicalis.
source: consistent with what has been reported in X. tropicalis (Gentsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Gentsch et al., 2019.

claim: Only 15% of genes exhibited deficient activation in Pou5f3/Sox3 morpholino-treated embryos.
source: RNA-seq of morpholino-treated embryos at stage 9 revealed extensive misregulation of genome activation, though only 15% of genes exhibited deficient activation
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 4A.

claim: 43% of genes exhibited slightly higher levels in Pou5f3/Sox3 morpholino-treated embryos.
source: while 43% of genes actually exhibited slightly higher levels in the morphants (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and G–K)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and G–K.

claim: Gene increases in Pou5f3/Sox3 morphants could be due to direct or indirect transcriptional repression mediated by Pou5f3 and Sox3.
source: which could be due to direct or indirect transcriptional repression mediated by Pou5f3 and Sox3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the up-regulation observed in morphants.

claim: Increases in gene expression in Pou5f3/Sox3 morphants were predominantly detected from intron signal.
source: Increases were predominantly detected from intron signal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J), which would largely rule out post-transcriptional effects.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: A larger proportion of strictly zygotic genes were down-regulated in the morphants compared to maternal-to-zygotic genes.
source: A larger proportion of strictly zygotic genes were down-regulated in the morphants compared to maternal-to-zygotic genes (p=6.6 × 10-18, χ-squared test, 3 d.o.f.), perhaps reflecting a more complex regulatory network that regulates maternal gene reactivation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis of RNA-seq data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Nearly 70% of first-wave genes were down regulated in Pou5f3/Sox3 morpholino-treated embryos with cycloheximide treatment.
source: In these embryos, nearly 70% of first-wave genes were down regulated, including the mir-427 transcript (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–F, I)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–F, I.

claim: Maternal Pou5f3 and Sox3 directly activate a large proportion of first-wave genome activation.
source: suggesting that maternal Pou5f3 and Sox3 directly activate a large proportion of first-wave genome activation, but newly synthesized zygotic factors rapidly mobilize to refine target gene expression levels (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the morpholino+cycloheximide RNA-seq data.

claim: Newly synthesized zygotic factors rapidly mobilize to refine target gene expression levels after initial Pou5f3/Sox3-mediated activation.
source: suggesting that maternal Pou5f3 and Sox3 directly activate a large proportion of first-wave genome activation, but newly synthesized zygotic factors rapidly mobilize to refine target gene expression levels (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the difference between morpholino effects with and without cycloheximide.

claim: In the absence of wild-type Pou5f3 and Sox3 activity, divergent homeolog activation is reduced for a subset of genes.
source: In the absence of wild-type Pou5f3 and Sox3 activity, divergent homeolog activation is reduced for a subset of genes, indicating that these factors at least partially underlie differential subgenome activation (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 4D–G.

claim: A significantly larger proportion of strictly zygotic genes encoded on both subgenomes is activated by Pou5f3 and Sox3 compared to singleton genes.
source: Among primary-activated genes, there does not seem to be a strong bias toward greater regulation of either homeolog; however, a significantly larger proportion of strictly zygotic genes encoded on both subgenomes is activated by Pou5f3 and Sox3 compared to singleton genes (p=0.0020, χ-squared test, 5 d.o.f.; Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, N)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis of RNA-seq data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, N.

claim: Peak calling revealed thousands of binding sites for Pou5f3 and Sox3 in X. laevis blastulae.
source: Peak calling revealed thousands of binding sites for each factor (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by CUT&RUN data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Homer de novo motif analysis recovered the OCT4 and SOX3 binding sequences as top hits in Pou5f3 and Sox3 CUT&RUN peaks.
source: and Homer de novo motif analysis recovered the OCT4 and SOX3 binding sequences as top hits (p=10–252 and p=10–104, respectively; Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by motif analysis in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: At least 10% of Pou5f3/Sox3 peaks contain matches to the Oct4-Sox2 heterodimer motif.
source: A subset of peaks have CUT&RUN enrichment for both factors, and at least 10% of peaks contain matches to the Oct4-Sox2 heterodimer motif (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by motif analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Pou5f3 and Sox3 may form a complex in the X. laevis blastula, similar to mammalian OCT4 and SOX2.
source: suggesting Pou5f3 and Sox3 may form a complex in the blastula, similar to mammalian OCT4 and SOX2 (Boyer et al., 2005; Dailey and Basilico, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the co-enrichment and dimer motif presence, with citations to Boyer et al., 2005 and Dailey and Basilico, 2001.

claim: CUT&RUN signal for Pou5f3 and Sox3 is enriched in the vicinity of genes down-regulated in morphants.
source: CUT&RUN signal for both factors is enriched in the vicinity of genes down-regulated in morphants with or without cycloheximide treatment, but notably not for genes up-regulated (p<1 × 10–43, Kruskal-Wallis test; Figure 4I and J)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by CUT&RUN data analysis in Figure 4I and J.

claim: Up-regulation of genes in Pou5f3/Sox3 morphants is likely an indirect effect of Pou5f3/Sox3 loss of function.
source: confirming that up regulation is likely an indirect effect of Pou5f3/Sox3 loss of function.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the lack of Pou5f3/Sox3 binding near up-regulated genes.

claim: Down-regulated genes are highly significantly nearer to predicted regulatory elements with enriched Pou5f3 and Sox3 binding.
source: Down-regulated genes are highly significantly nearer to predicted regulatory elements with enriched Pou5f3 and Sox3 binding (p<1 × 10–300, Kruskal-Wallis test; Figure 4K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 4K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Differential Pou5f3 and Sox3 binding mirrors differential predicted enhancer activity.
source: Differential Pou5f3 and Sox3 binding mirrors differential predicted enhancer activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by CUT&RUN data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Subgenome-specific Pou5f3 and Sox3 binding is enriched in the vicinity of the homeolog affected by Pou5f3/Sox3 loss of function.
source: and subgenome-specific Pou5f3 and Sox3 binding is enriched in the vicinity of the homeolog affected by Pou5f3/Sox3 loss of function (p=7.9 × 10–13, Kruskal-Wallis test; Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Pou5f3.3 and Sox3 regulate ZGA differentially between the two X. laevis subgenomes.
source: Together, these results implicate Pou5f3.3 and Sox3 in regulating ZGA differentially between the two subgenomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the CUT&RUN and morpholino data.

claim: There is broad conservation of relative expression levels between X. tropicalis and X. laevis embryonic transcriptomes after genome activation when X. laevis homeolog levels are summed gene-wise.
source: For three-way homeologs/orthologs that are strictly zygotic in X. laevis, there is broad conservation of relative expression levels between the X. tropicalis and X. laevis embryonic transcriptomes after genome activation, when X. laevis homeolog levels are summed gene-wise (Spearman's ρ=0.67) (Figure 5A, left, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The correlation between X. tropicalis and X. laevis expression weakens when the X. laevis subgenomes are considered independently.
source: However, the correlation weakens when the X. laevis subgenomes are considered independently: relative activation levels in one subgenome alone are depressed relative to X. tropicalis, with expression of some genes completely restricted to one subgenome or the other (L, Spearman's ρ=0.56; S, ρ=0.47; Figure 5A, middle, right, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparative RNA-seq analysis in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The X. tropicalis embryonic transcriptome is a better estimator for the composite X. laevis transcriptome than for either subtranscriptome individually.
source: Indeed, the X. tropicalis embryonic transcriptome is a better estimator for the composite X. laevis transcriptome than for either subtranscriptome individually (p<4.3 × 10–13 for strictly zygotic genes, p<1.4 × 10–83 for maternal-zygotic genes, Wilcoxon signed-rank test on residuals; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: X. laevis underwent regulatory changes post allotetraploidization that maintained relative gene expression dosage for embryonic genome activation.
source: If the diploid L and S progenitor embryos each exhibited the inferred ancestral activation levels, then these trends strongly suggest that X. laevis underwent regulatory changes post allotetraploidization that maintained relative gene expression dosage for embryonic genome activation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the comparative transcriptome analysis.

claim: Genes activated from both X. laevis homeologs are more likely to have orthologous X. tropicalis activation.
source: When we specifically compare zygotic activation between the two species, genes activated from both X. laevis homeologs are more likely to have orthologous X. tropicalis activation (p=1.7 × 10–44, χ-squared test, 4 d.o.f.; Figure 5B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Genes activated from both X. laevis homeologs are more likely to have conserved X. tropicalis Pou5f3/Sox3 regulation.
source: as well as conserved X. tropicalis Pou5f3/Sox3 regulation (p<1.7 × 10–6, χ-squared test, 8 d.o.f.; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; Gentsch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D with citation to Gentsch et al., 2019.

claim: Many differentially activated homeologs have acquired novel ZGA regulation by Pou5f3 and Sox3 compared to the inferred ancestral state.
source: This suggests that many differentially activated homeologs have acquired novel ZGA regulation by Pou5f3 and Sox3 compared to the inferred ancestral state.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the conservation analysis.

claim: Subgenome-specific predicted enhancers are less likely to be conserved with X. tropicalis.
source: Predicted enhancers also follow this trend: subgenome-specific predicted enhancers are less likely to be conserved with X. tropicalis (p=1.5 × 10–76, χ-squared test for high confidence enhancers, 4 d.o.f; Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Greater regulatory innovation underlies differentially activated homeologs in X. laevis.
source: consistent with a greater degree of regulatory innovation underlying differentially activated homeologs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the lower conservation of subgenome-specific enhancers.

claim: Genes activated in X. laevis are largely also expressed in zebrafish embryos.
source: We find that genes activated in X. laevis are largely also expressed in zebrafish embryos (~450 million years separated) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by comparative analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Co-activated X. laevis homeologs are more likely to be part of the first wave of zebrafish genome activation.
source: Despite considerable divergence in activation timing, co-activated X. laevis homeologs are still more likely to be part of the first wave of zebrafish genome activation (p=4.3 × 10–12, χ-squared test, 4 d.o.f.)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Co-activated X. laevis homeologs are more likely to be targeted by zebrafish maternal homologs of OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG.
source: and targeted by zebrafish maternal homologs of OCT4 and SOX2, but also NANOG (p=1.8 × 10–45, χ-squared test, 6 d.o.f.) (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Subgenome-shared predicted enhancers are more likely to have evidence for conservation in zebrafish.
source: Subgenome-shared predicted enhancers are also more likely to have evidence for conservation in zebrafish (p=2.8 × 10–58 for all enhancers, p=5.0 × 10–4 for high-confidence enhancers, χ-squared tests, 4 d.o.f.) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H; Bogdanovic et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H with citation to Bogdanovic et al., 2012.

claim: The regulatory architecture underlying differential homeolog activation in X. laevis is more likely to be derived.
source: Taken together, this suggests that the regulatory architecture underlying differential homeolog activation in X. laevis is more likely to be derived, in contrast to the deeply conserved networks that regulate many co-activated homeologs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the conservation analyses with X. tropicalis and zebrafish.

claim: Xenopus and possibly all Anuran amphibians lack a NANOG ortholog.
source: Interestingly, Xenopus and possibly all Anuran amphibians lack a NANOG ortholog, likely due to a chromosomal deletion (Schuff et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Schuff et al., 2012.

claim: Maternal Pou5f3.3 and Sox3 have subsumed NANOG's roles in X. laevis genome activation.
source: In the absence of a Nanog homolog in the maternal contribution, we find that maternal Pou5f3.3 and Sox3 seem to have subsumed NANOG's roles in X. laevis genome activation
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the functional data and the absence of NANOG.

claim: Zygotic factors such as Ventx help promote cell potency in the early X. laevis gastrula.
source: while zygotic factors such as Ventx help promote cell potency in the early gastrula (Scerbo et al., 2012; Schuff et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Scerbo et al., 2012 and Schuff et al., 2012.

claim: There is core-vertebrate mechanistic conservation in genome activation amid both cis- and trans-regulatory shuffling.
source: This demonstrates core-vertebrate mechanistic conservation in genome activation amid both cis- and trans-regulatory shuffling, which converge to support pluripotent stem cell induction and embryonic development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the comparative analyses.

claim: Pou5f3.3 and Sox3 are maternal activators of embryonic genome activation in X. laevis.
source: Together, our findings establish the pluripotency factors Pou5f3.3 and Sox3 as maternal activators of embryonic genome activation
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the main findings.

claim: Pou5f3.3 and Sox3 are differentially recruited to the two homeologous subgenomes of X. laevis by a rewired enhancer network.
source: which are differentially recruited to the two homeologous subgenomes of X. laevis by a rewired enhancer network (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of the main findings, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: A majority of annotated homeolog pairs experience differential activation during the MZT in X. laevis.
source: Of the thousands of genes activated during the MZT, a majority of annotated homeolog pairs experience differential activation
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Differential activation in X. laevis appears to be driven by subgenome-specific enhancer gain and/or loss correlated with differential Pou5f3.3/Sox3 binding and regulation.
source: which appears to be driven by subgenome-specific enhancer gain and/or loss correlated with differential Pou5f3.3/Sox3 binding and regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The magnitude of regulatory divergence between X. laevis subgenomes has had a net neutral effect on the composite reprogrammed embryonic transcriptome.
source: However, this magnitude of regulatory divergence seems to have had a net neutral effect, as combined subgenome activation produces a composite reprogrammed embryonic transcriptome akin to diploid X. tropicalis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the comparative transcriptome data.

claim: Regulatory divergence between the X. laevis subgenomes is likely even broader as embryogenesis proceeds.
source: As embryogenesis proceeds, regulatory divergence between the subgenomes is likely even broader.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as speculation based on the observed trends.

claim: In X. tropicalis, signal transducers and transcription factors including Pou5f3.2/3, Sox3, Smad1/2, β-catenin, Vegt, Otx1, and Foxh1 regulate embryo-wide and regional gene activation.
source: In X. tropicalis, signal transducers and transcription factors including Pou5f3.2/3, Sox3, Smad1/2, β-catenin, Vegt, Otx1, and Foxh1 regulate embryo-wide and regional gene activation (Charney et al., 2017; Gentsch et al., 2019; Paraiso et al., 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Charney et al., 2017; Gentsch et al., 2019; Paraiso et al., 2019.

claim: Binding motifs for some X. tropicalis transcription factors are found in differentially active X. laevis enhancers.
source: and binding motifs for some of these are found in differentially active X. laevis enhancers (Figure 3F, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by motif analysis in Figure 3F and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Focusing on accessible chromatin in animal caps may have underestimated the magnitude of homeologous enhancer divergence regulating endodermal fate in vegetal cells.
source: Additionally, by focusing on accessible chromatin in animal caps, we may have underestimated the magnitude of homeologous enhancer divergence regulating endodermal fate in the vegetal cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a limitation of the study.

claim: Subgenome regulatory differences in X. laevis converge to producing ancestral dosages in the transcriptome.
source: But based on the close morphological similarity of X. tropicalis and X. laevis embryos, we would predict that these subgenome regulatory differences also converge to producing ancestral dosages in the transcriptome.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a prediction based on morphological similarity.

claim: Homeolog expression bias can derive from gene regulatory differences evolved in the parental species prior to hybridization.
source: Although homeolog expression bias can derive from gene regulatory differences evolved in the parental species prior to hybridization (Buggs et al., 2014; Grover et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with citations to Buggs et al., 2014 and Grover et al., 2012.

claim: Regulatory upheaval in X. laevis post-hybridization led to expression level gain or loss in one homeolog, which was subsequently corrected by compensatory changes to the other homeolog.
source: we propose that regulatory upheaval in X. laevis post-hybridization (i.e. 'genome shock' McClintock, 1984) led to expression level gain or loss in one homeolog, which was subsequently corrected by compensatory changes to the other homeolog, possibly repeatedly (Shi et al., 2012; Tirosh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a proposed model with citations to McClintock, 1984; Shi et al., 2012; Tirosh et al., 2009.

claim: Early development exerts constraint on the reprogrammed embryonic transcriptome while tolerating regulatory turnover.
source: This implies that early development exerts constraint on the reprogrammed embryonic transcriptome while tolerating (or facilitating) regulatory turnover.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the proposed model.

claim: The reconfiguration of the mir-427 cluster highlights how essential MZT regulatory mechanisms can evolve neutrally.
source: The apparent reconfiguration of the mir-427 cluster after the X. laevis and tropicalis lineages split similarly highlights how essential MZT regulatory mechanisms can evolve, ostensibly neutrally given that miR-427-directed maternal clearance is conserved in Xenopus.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the mir-427 findings.

claim: X. laevis embryos illustrate how the pluripotency program may have accommodated regulatory network disruptions, genomic instability, and aneuploidy across the animal tree.
source: Thus, X. laevis embryos illustrate how the pluripotency program may have accommodated regulatory network disruptions, genomic instability, and aneuploidy across the animal tree.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a broader implication of the findings.
